qs.q: Which statement about the pot still is correct?
o: It must be emptied and cleaned after each distillation
It can run continuously without ever stopping
It easily produces neutral spirits at 96% abv
It is a vertical structure divided into many sections
qs.e: Continuous running, neutral strengths and a tall structure divided into sections all describe the column still. However many times it is used, a pot still never reaches a very high-strength neutral spirit.

qs.q: Where does the sweetness you taste in a spirit come from?
o: From the raw material's sugar passing through the still
From the water used for dilution
qs.e: The raw material's sugar is eaten by yeast and does not travel with the vapours anyway. Caramel colouring is not sweet. Dilution water is pure and brings neither flavour nor sugar.

qs.q: A distiller is using a raw material that contains no sugar. What must happen?
o: Process it to create sugar before fermentation
Distil it directly without fermenting it
Add extra yeast, which replaces the sugar
Age it in oak so it develops sugar
qs.e: Without fermentation there is no alcohol to concentrate, so distilling straight away would make no sense. Yeast does not replace sugar: it eats it. Oak comes after distillation and creates no sugar to ferment.

qs.q: Which flavouring technique also gives the spirit colour?
qs.e: Redistilling with plants gives a flavoured but colourless liquid, because colour does not travel with the vapours. Dilution uses pure water. A column still is for distilling, not flavouring.

qs.q: What does the term VS guarantee on a Cognac?
qs.e: 4 years is the minimum for VSOP and 10 years for XO. Six months is below the legal minimum: a spirit that young cannot even be called Cognac.

qs.q: Which type of still is essential for making vodka?
qs.e: Some producers use pot stills for part of the process, but on their own they cannot reach a neutral spirit. Fermentation stops at around 8–10%. A barrel is not a still, and vodka is not aged in oak.

qs.q: During malting, what does barley produce as it grows?
qs.e: The enzymes really get to work once the crushed barley is mixed with water. Yeast, by contrast, is added later to the sugary liquid. Smoke does not come from sprouting: it only appears if peat is burned while the barley is heated.

qs.q: What character does unmalted barley give some Irish pot-still whiskeys?
o: Nutty notes and an oily texture
qs.e: It is an unusual ingredient, used only in some Irish whiskeys made in pot stills. Smoke comes from peat, pepper from rye, and sweetcorn and coconut from corn and new barrels as in Bourbon.

qs.q: Many Caribbean distilleries own both pot stills and columns. Why is that useful?
o: To have spirits of different intensities to blend
Because the law requires two distillations
Because columns are used for ageing
Because the pot still is used to sweeten
qs.e: With several types of spirit, blenders can create very different products, also combining different ages and distilleries. No general Caribbean rule requires two distillations. Columns are for distilling, not ageing, and sugar is added afterwards, not in the still.

qs.q: How are the best Tequilas distilled?
o: Twice in pot stills, to a low strength
Once in a tall column, to 96% abv
Three times in columns, to a high strength
Once in a pot still, then charcoal filtered
qs.e: The lower the strength, the more aroma stays in the spirit. A tall column reaching 96% abv makes a neutral spirit, the opposite of what is wanted. Charcoal filtering is not part of the typical Tequila method; it belongs rather to Tennessee whiskey or some white rums.

qs.q: What does the law say about sugar in liqueurs?
o: There must be a minimum level of sweetness
Sugar may only come from fruit
qs.e: Sugar is not just allowed but required, so it cannot be banned or optional. It is added after flavouring and does not have to come from fruit.

qs.q: Which list gives the four components of every aromatised wine?
o: Wine, flavourings incl. a bitter, sugar, spirit
qs.e: Caramel is only optional and soda water does not belong. Spirit, cream and colourings describe a cream liqueur instead. Juice and yeast are not part of the recipe, and that list leaves out the spirit, which is required.

qs.q: A wine spirit from the Cognac area, distilled by the rules, has spent 18 months in oak. Can it be sold as Cognac?
o: No, it needs at least two years in oak
Yes, as long as it was distilled twice
qs.e: VS is the youngest term but still requires at least 2 years. Double distillation is compulsory but does not replace ageing. Caramel only changes the colour, not the age.

qs.q: What happens to vodka after distillation?
o: It stays unaged and is diluted, usually to 40% abv
It ages for at least two years in oak
It is bottled at 96% abv without dilution
It is always sweetened with sugar
qs.e: Two years in oak describes Cognac, not vodka. At 96% it would be undrinkable, as such strong alcohol numbs the palate. Sweetening is not part of vodka's basic recipe.

qs.q: A whisky is distilled in Scotland, then aged four years in England. Can it be called Scotch?
o: No: the ageing must also take place in Scotland
Yes: only the place of distillation counts
Yes, as long as it is made from malted barley
No: Scotch must age for ten years
qs.e: Four years would be long enough, but the place is wrong. The grain used does not change this rule, which applies to every Scotch. The minimum is three years, not ten: the only problem here is geography.

qs.q: Where can Tennessee whiskey be made?
o: Only in the state of Tennessee
qs.e: It is Bourbon that can be made anywhere in the USA. Kentucky is the heart of Bourbon, not of Tennessee whiskey. Charcoal filtering is necessary but not enough: without the right place, the name cannot be used.

qs.q: Which statement about adding sugar to rum is correct?
o: Common in Central and South America, banned in some countries
Happens on its own during ageing
qs.e: The rules change from country to country, so neither a requirement nor a ban applies everywhere. Every spirit is dry when it leaves the still: sweetness only comes from sugar added after distillation, not from the barrel.

qs.q: Why are aged Tequilas rarely matured for very long?
o: To keep oak from masking the agave character
Because the law forbids more than a year in oak
Because the Mexican climate evaporates it all
qs.e: It is a style choice, not a ban: Añejo, for example, has a 12-month minimum and no maximum. The other two answers have no basis: the aim is for oak to support the agave, not dominate it.

qs.q: How are flavoured vodkas usually made?
qs.e: The base is the same neutral vodka, not a fruit spirit. Oak plays no part, and sugar plus caramel would lead to a coloured liqueur, not a flavoured vodka.

qs.q: Which areas are best known for aromatised wines?
qs.e: The second answer flips the directions. Scotland and Ireland point to whisky, Mexico and the Caribbean to Tequila and rum: those are spirits, while this is about wine-based products.

qs.q: What must be done to molasses before it can ferment?
qs.e: Sprouting belongs to malting grain for whisky. Cooking in ovens is how sugar is created from agave cores for Tequila. Charcoal filtering comes after distillation, for example to remove colour from rum.

qs.q: In a tasting note, what does the 'finish' describe?
o: How long the flavours linger after spitting
The colour of the liquid at the bottom of the glass
The last aroma noticed before adding water
The alcoholic strength shown on the label
qs.e: The finish is the last observation on the palate: after spitting, you note how long the flavours last. A long finish is often a sign of quality. Colour belongs to appearance, aromas to the nose, and alcoholic strength is label information, not a tasting observation.

qs.q: In a short drink stirred with ice and served with nothing added, where does the 'weak' element come from?
o: From water as the ice melts during stirring
From the bitters added by the dash
From the citrus peel used as a garnish
qs.e: In short drinks, dilution comes almost entirely from ice during mixing, by stirring or shaking. Bitters are a bitter accent, the spirit is the strong part and a citrus peel adds scent, but none of them really lengthens the drink.

qs.q: Why is the Americano said to have a 'split base'?
o: Its alcoholic part is Campari and sweet vermouth together
It is served half in a short glass and half in a tall one
It mixes lemon juice and lime juice
qs.e: Instead of a single spirit, the Americano uses two alcoholic ingredients that together form the base, then lengthened with club soda. It contains no gin and no citrus: think of a Negroni without the gin, made long with soda.

qs.q: In a cocktail, what makes up the 'strong' element?
qs.e: The strong element brings the alcohol and the main character of the drink. Citrus gives acidity, syrup gives sweetness and ice gives dilution, which belongs to the weak side: they are counterweights, not the base.
